messages.subject: Fit of a complex bivariate model
messages.subject_clean: Fit of a complex bivariate model
messages.body_plain:
Hello everybody,

I am currently trying to fit a bivariate model using a continuous-space process with INLA. The model is quite hard to conceptualise, and so I started thinking about the model I would like to fit as a discrete-time process. I have simulated data and can recover the parameters using INLA. The models for the two responses Y1 and Y2 at time t are :

Y1_[t] = eta_[t] + e1_[t]     with       eta_[t] = X_[t]*beta+u[t]

where eta is a linear predictor  and e1 is a residual. The linear predictor has a fixed effect part X_[t]*beta and a random effect part u[t], and the random effects follow an AR1 process:

u[t] = rho1*u[t-1]+eu[t]

where rho1 is the autoregression parameter and eu[t] the 'innovation' residual. This is quite straightforward. However, the model for Y2 is :

Y2_[t] = b*eta_[t] + rho2*eta_[t-1] + e2_[t]

where b and rho2 are the regression coefficients associated with Y1's linear predictor at time t and t-1 respectively. I have attached the R code that fit this model. I have applied the method used in ''The R-INLA tutorial on SPDE models'' - Chap. 18 - Copying part or the entire linear predictor - p. 128 - 133 : https://www.math.ntnu.no/inla/r-inla.org/tutorials/spde/spde-tutorial.pdf

What I want to do is to adapt this model to continuous space, but I am having trouble constructing the model. The three difficulties are :

a) space is continuous not discrete

b) time only moves forward, whereas space is bidirectional and so really eta_[t-1] should be treated the same as  eta_[t+1] in the model for Y2 (if space was 1 dimensional and discrete)

c) space is 2D rather than 1

Is it possible to fit the spatial analogue of the temporal model I describe with INLA ?

Thanks for your help,

Cheers,

Pierre

messages.body_plain:
On 01/09/2017 07:52 AM, pierre...@hotmail.fr wrote:
>
> Y2_[t] = b*eta_[t] + rho2*eta_[t-1] + e2_[t]

The example in the tutorial is for the continuous spatial domain. However, it only copies the spatial field at the same position. A way to copy it including nearby elements will be to include an adequate A matrix.

Following the example in the tutorial, the third data stack will have an additional A matrix:

stack3 <- inla.stack(tag='y3',
   data=list(y=y3),
   effects=list(list(eta2c=1:n, e3=1:n), eta2n),
   A=list(1, A.special))

where A.special will serves to collect the terms at some neighbourhood. Additionally, the formula will have an additional term such f(eta2n, copy='eta2', fixed=FALSE).

This is a generalization of the copying temporally lagged index strategy in http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0167947311003999 and better explained in the last chapter of https://sites.google.com/a/r-inla.org/stbook/

Elias

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am very new to INLA, so my upfront apologies if this question sounds silly.

I am trying to implement INLA, but I would like to provide some evidence in my choice for the data likelihood, in here <http://www.r-inla.org/models/likelihoods>

Therefore, I would like to know if there's any statistic test that I could apply to test my data against the likelihood models in INLA.

I've been doing it with fitdist function from fitdistrplus package, but it doesnt have all the distributions that INLA has, that's why my question.

Thanks in advance if anyone can give me a light on this one.

On 16 Jan 2017, at 15:39, Paul Lantos <paul....@gmail.com> wrote:

> Looks like for some reason I'm getting NAs in g.mean and g.sd <http://g.sd>

Yes, your mesh has

xlim: -79.43167 -78.27963
ylim: 35.39146 36.56701

but your projection used xlim=c(0, 1) and ylim=c(0, 1), so you'll
need to change that.  The simplest option is to not specify xlim and
ylim for inla.mesh.projector(), which will make it use the mesh limits instead.
You only need to specify them if you want finer control.

You may also want to use gproj$x and gproj$y in the levelplot calls if you want
to have meaningful axes.

Finn

Some of Finn's old plotting code (obviously won't run, but it should tell you where to put things):

levelplot(row.values=proj$x, column.values=proj$y, x=plotdata,
                 mm=mm, panel=levelplotmap,
                 col.regions=my.palette,
                 xlim=range(proj$x), ylim=range(proj$y), aspect="iso",
                 contour=TRUE, cuts=11, labels=FALSE, pretty=TRUE,
                 xlab="Easting",ylab="Northing")

Dan

Thanks again -
 Might be best if I could figure it out in ggplot2, or better yet compile x, y, mean, and sd into a data frame I can use in GIS.

 I have a couple other parallel questions if you don't mind - I'm using this analysis as an alternative to generalized additive modeling, with a smoothed term for the x,y coordinate pairs. I'd like to figure out how to do the following things that I can do using GAMs (this would come after doing a prediction to a grid):

1 - calculate pointwise / local odds ratios comparing the local odds prediction to the global odds (i.e. the same model but without spatial terms). I'm assuming that I can leave the f(spatial, model=spde) part out of the formula to get a global model, then if it's predicted in log-odds just subtract the local from the global odds predictions at each point?

2 - draw "significance" contours where local odds is significantly different from global odds. I'm still trying to wrap my head around what this means in a Bayesian context!

Thanks for any help,
Paul

messages.body_plain:
Short answer for now:
The models in inla are GAMs, they just have "Bayesian" in front. ;-)

1. Yes, you can make linear combination in the log-scale and get the posteriors.
2. Yes. The "excursions" package and associated papers by Bolin & Lindgren
Is meant for such things, and can interpret inla output.

Finn

>
> 1 - calculate pointwise / local odds ratios comparing the local odds prediction to the global odds (i.e. the same model but without spatial terms). messages.body_plain:
Some more plotting code (this time from me).

Here adm0 is a  SpatialPolygonsDataFrame that I want to clip the spatial plot to.

Again, code won't compile (and is ugly) but it might be useful.

D

proj = inla.mesh.projector(mesh,dims=c(200,200))
S = result$summary.fitted.values$mean[ind.fit]

field.plot = inla.mesh.project(proj,field=S,dims=c(200,200))

x = proj$x
y=proj$y
all = (expand.grid(x,y,KEEP.OUT.ATTRS = F))
names(all) = c("x","y")

plotdata = all %>%mutate(field = round(as.numeric(field.plot)) )

coordinates(plotdata)=~x+y #make plotdata a spatialPointsDataFrame!

##adm0 is a SpatialPolygonsDataFrame
#the points need to have the same coordinate system.
#there's almost certainly a better way to do this

plotdata@proj4string = adm0@proj4string
ppp=plotdata[adm0,] #this is it! subset the SpatialPoints object by the polygon!!

plotdata.clip= as.data.frame(ppp)

ggplot(plotdata.clip,aes(x,y)) + geom_tile(aes(fill=field))

When I run INLA using a binomial formula for a dichotomous outcome variable, are the values of the posterior mean log-odds?

Thanks,
Paul

messages.body_plain:
Hmmm, in a binomial model the linear predictor is in logit-scale.
I'm not sure what the log-odds are in the model.

The x and y coordinate for spatial variables are used when defining
the predictor and are not themselves present in the output.

Usually, a "prediction stack" can be used, and inla.stack.index() be
used to extract the required indices needed for extracting the
corresponding values from summary.linear.predictor and/or summary.fitted.values.

So can I use this function on the posterior estimate to generate probabilities, then convert those to odds, i.e. antilogit(x) / (1 - antilogit(x))? This is from the R-INLA book:

I've spent quite some time with your excellent paper!

The prediction code I'm using, which looks similar, is from the R-INLA book:

tcoo <- rbind(c(0.3, 0.3), c(0.5, 0.5), c(0.7, 0.7))
Ap <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = cmv.mesh, loc = tcoo)
x0 <- c(0.5, 0.5, 0.5)
stk.pred <- inla.stack(tag='pred', A=list(Ap, 1), data=list(y=NA), ## response as NA
                       effects=list(s=1:cmv.spde$n.spde, data.frame(x=x0, b0=1)))
stk.full <- inla.stack(stk.e, stk.pred)
p.res <- inla(formula_1a, data=inla.stack.data(stk.full), ## full stack
              control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE, ## compute the predictor
                                     A=inla.stack.A(stk.full))) ## using full stack data

pred.ind <- inla.stack.index(stk.full, tag = "pred")$data
ypost <- p.res$marginals.fitted.values[pred.ind]

Still, I think what I'm having difficulty with here is 1) getting the posterior mean and sd into a form I understand, 2) attaching them to their corresponding coordinate pairs in a grid, and 3) getting those into a format I can export.

This is how I make predictions using GAMs. In that case I just manually make a say 100x100 grid, then predict the GAM to the grid:

row=100
col=100
grid=as.data.frame(expand.grid(x=seq(from=min(x), to=max(x),len=col),
                                  y=seq(from=min(y),to=max(y),len=row)))
gam1<-gam(result ~ s(x,y), family = binomial(logit))
grid$pred <- predict(gam1, grid)

That gets me all I need to export it as a table to GIS. If I have additional predictors in the model, say result ~ s(x,y) + age, I add a column with median age to the grid. I assume I would do the same using inla.stack for a grid with predictors?

messages.body_plain:
Hi again,

 I'm running a set of models in which I've got observations at 19,000 coordinate pairs. I've created a grid over the study area to make predictions at unmeasured sites, because the data are not evenly distributed -- so all in all I have 26,000 points, 19k of which have observations and 7k are NA.

 I've compiled the observations and the grid into a single data frame, which I use to define the coords object for a binomial SPDE model. For the unobserved points I have reference values for covariates, so there are no NA values in predictors.

 Here is the model structure - this is the base model with no covariates:

formula_1 <- y ~ 0 + b0 + x
  f(s, model=hearing.spde) + f(fips, model = "iid")
model_1 <- inla(formula_1,
                 data=inla.stack.data(stk.e), family="binomial",
                 control.predictor=list(A =inla.stack.A(stk.e), compute=TRUE),
                 control.compute = list(dic = TRUE))
summary(model_1)

Having fitted the model, I've tried to tack the posterior mean and sd back to the coordinates, but I get the following problem:

> predictions<-data.frame(coords, m.prd, sd.prd)

Error in data.frame(coords, m.prd, sd.prd) :

  arguments imply differing number of rows: 26089, 54142

> dim(coords)
[1] 26089     2
> dim(model_1$summary.fitted.values)
[1] 54142     6

Would appreciate any help.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Paul,

your code for extracting m.prd and sd.prd are not in your email, and that's where the problem likely lies.

"stk.e" sounds suspiciously like an "estimation" stack; we often build the stack for the inla() by joining an "estimation" stack with a "prediction" stack.
By doing it that way, we can use the "tag" argument to inla.stack to keep track of where in the output the predictions will be found; the predictor variables will include both those for the estimation data, and for the desired predictions, and the inla.stack.index() function keeps track of this.

The code structure becomes something like this:

stk.est <- inla.stack(..., tag="estimation")
stk.pred <- inla.stack(..., tag="prediction")
stk <- inla.stack(stk.est, stk.pred)
...
model <- inla(...)
m.prd <- model$summary.fitted.values[inla.stack.index(stk, "prediction")$data, "mean"]
sd.prd <- model$summary.fitted.values[inla.stack.index(stk, "prediction")$data, "sd"]

Finn

messages.body_plain:
your grid doesn't have a parity_std slot, that you try to use. Note that the error message refers to the data.frame() call, so it hasn't even reached the inla.stack code.

Your inla.stack syntax is also slightly off; each A-matrix should have an associated list() in the effects parameter. It tries to do its best to interpret the input, but some things it will fail on, so it's better to follow the documented syntax. In your case list(list(...), list(...)).   The howto should be corrected if it doesn't do that...

Finn

On 18 January 2017 at 12:39, Paul Lantos <paul....@gmail.com> wrote:

> Right, that was the typo, I had parity bit not parity_std (the standardized variable). I've made the variable name "parity" in both data and grid now. I also added list:

Yes,  I only saw your note about that after I sent the reply.

> The How To isn't quite clear on the 'list', I think because it's a simpler example model. I assume in this case that b0=1 is intercept and x=x is meant to be some linear predictor?

Yes. The howto uses a simplified syntax that works in that case, but is probably best avoided in general.

> 1 - I'd like to run non-spatial versions of the same models in order to compare local vs global odds. To do this do I simply leave f(s, model=spde) out of the formula?

Essentially yes, but you'll want to remove the spde-related parts from the stack as well to avoid a needlessly large internal model (it might even complain if you don't).

> 2 - The output I'm going for is an odds ratio, so at any given point I divide local by global odds. I assume that if the posterior mean is on a logit scale, I can do an antilogit to get probability, then convert probability to odds by p / (1-p), then do the ratio?

For the odds itself you could do that. The log-odds is actually the logit of the probability, logit(p) = log(p) - log(1-p) = log( p/(1-p) ), so taking the exponential of the linear.predictor quantiles will give you quantiles of the odds.  But as soon as you start looking at quantities that depend on multiple values of the predictor (local and global in this case), you have to take the dependence into account. A general way of doing that is to sample from the posterior with inla.posterior.sample(), compute whatever non-linear function of the samples you desire, and extract the summary statistics/empirical cdf etc from that. But again, the ratio between the odds is the exponential of the difference in logit-probability, so it might be possible to formulate the log-ratio as another linear predictor in the inla call.  But I don't work with odds ratio models, so I have no idea what that would look like, sorry...
One option is of course to ignore the dependence, but that might be dangerous...

>
> 3 - I would like to have contours circumscribing areas where the difference between local and global odds is "significant" -- a concept easier to wrap my head around in frequentist terms. If I understand correctly, in a Bayesian scheme would this be where the local posterior density has only 5% overlap with the global posterior density? How do I compute that?

If you only need pointwise significance, then you can evaluate pointwise "p-like"-values via the pointwise posterior marginal distributions of the log-odds-ratios (if those can be obtained as mentioned above).  2*min(P(X<0), P(X>0)), where X=log(oddsratio) I believe.

Finn

> To remove the spde-related parts from the stack that would mean removing the highlighted component? Do I leave in A.est? I get an error when I try to run inla.stack after removing either or both.

Remove both.
But try the more strict syntax for effects, and without the data frame:
  A=list(1),
  effects=list(list(b0=1, x1=x1, x2=x2))

If you still get some error, please copy the error message. They are usually actually informative...

The overall mean is a dense linear combination, and getting the marginals for the differences will be a bit more tricky with this prediction approach. You could use the other linear combination method to get the posterior for the overall mean, but it wouldn't provide the posterior for the differences.
The sampling approach would allow you to do "the right thing".
Or just take a point estimate for the "null" as the average of the point estimates. That would probably be very similar...

Finn

The warning message says there is something wrong with the Rcpp package in your R installation, so I'd look at that before trying to run the inla code, as it appears you're running some inla code that uses that package.

R only displays warnings after the code has terminated, which is why the warning shows up only after the error message. So if you get an error and then a warning, often the warning indicates the root cause, and the error is just an effect of that.

messages.body_plain:
On 18 January 2017 at 19:18, Paul Lantos <paul....@gmail.com> wrote:

> How is the posterior sampling different from just making a grid using:
>
> m.prd<- model_1$summary.fitted.values$mean
> sd.prd<- model_1$summary.fitted.values$sd
> predictions<-data.frame(grid.coords, m.prd)

I becomes relevant when you're evaluating something more complex, like the difference between the value at a point, and the overall average:
For a spatial model x(s) on a domain D, the marginal conditional expectations and variances (in the form of std.dev <http://std.dev>.) are what you get from the inla call:

m(s) = E(x(s) | Y)
sd(s)^2 = Var(x(s) | Y)

But if you want the posterior for

z(s) := x(s) - \int_u x(u) du / |D|

i.e. the difference between x(s) and its spatial average, then only the expectation is easy:

E(z(s) | Y) = E(x(s) | Y) - \int_u E(x(u) | Y) du / |D| = m(s) - \int_u m(u) du / |D|

For the variances, we get

Var(z(s) | Y) = Var(x(s)) - 2 \int_u Cov(x(s), x(u)) du / |D| + \int_u \int_v Cov(x(u), x(v)) dv du / |D|^2

where only the first term involves the marginal variances for x(s); the two other terms are integrals over the posterior covariances, which are not available.

But by sampling K times from the joint posterior, giving samples of the entire field x^[k](.) ~ (x(.) | Y), which inla.posterior.sample() does, you get the Monte Carlo estimate of each Var(z(s) | Y) via

z^[k](s) = x^[k](s) - \int_u x^[k](u) du / |D|
Var(z(s) | Y) \approx 1/K \sum_{k=1}^K (z^[k](s) - E(z(s) | Y))^2

without needing explicit access to the covariances.

This also allows non-linear functionals to be handled.

Of course, the situation changes if the z(s) you are interested in are

z(s) := x(s) - \int_u m(u) du / |D|

which is just a shift of x(s) with the spatial average of the posterior mean for x(s).  In that case, nothing interesting happens...
I'm not sure which of the two is the relevant one in a Bayesian log-odds-ratio analysis.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Only you have the coordinates; they aren't used by the inla() call, which only needs the A-matrix information, that encodes the relationship between the model and the observations.

You had it almost correct earlier; you just need to use the stack index information as well:

m.prd<- model_1$summary.fitted.values[inla.stack.index(stack, "predictor")$data,"mean"]
sd.prd<- model_1$summary.fitted.values[inla.stack.index(stack, "predictor")$data,"sd"]
predictions<-data.frame(grid.coords, mean=m.prd, sd=sd.prd)
​
Finn

>  I then need a way to circumscribe significant areas of the grid, i.e. showing in some form or another where the spatial heterogeneity is signfiicant. Trying to figure that out using excursions, but haven't made much progress yet.

The excursions package is meant for joint posterior probabilities, so that falls squarely under "complexities".
For pointwise "significance",
  m <- mean(m.prd) ## sensible since you're predicting onto a uniform lattice
  pvalue <- 2*pmin(pnorm(m, m.prd, sd.prd), 1-pnorm(m, m.prd, sd.prd))
gives you a kind of Bayesian pointwise two-sided p-values. (H0: x(s)=m)
This ignores the complexities of dependence and non-Gaussian posteriors and having a null hypothesis that depends on the data, but at least it's simple...

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I've been running a spatio temporal model in R-INLA. the time scope is 46 years, and it's yearly data.

The models run pretty smoothly for the Knorr-Held formulation described in "spatio and spatio-temporal bayesian models with R-INLA", with the following code:

control <- list(
  predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
  results = list(return.marginals.random = TRUE, return.marginals.predictor=TRUE),
  compute = list(hyperpar=TRUE, return.marginals=TRUE, dic=TRUE, mlik = TRUE, cpo = TRUE,
                 po = TRUE, waic=TRUE, graph=TRUE, gdensity=TRUE, openmp.strategy="huge"),
  group = list(model="rw2"))

#non-parametric dynamic trend
#knorr-held formulation
formula2 <- numberTorn ~1 + f(ID, model = "bym", graph=tornb.inla) + f(Year, model="crw2")+
  f(Year2, model="iid")
modelsptp2 <- inla(formula = formula2, family = "poisson",
                   quantiles = c(.05, .5, .95),
                   data = TornInla,
                   control.compute = control$compute,
                   control.predictor = control$predictor)
summary(modelsptp2)

But I also would like to understand the space-time interactions, so I started to dig into it, and this is what happens:

#SP-TIME INTERACTION
#TYPE I
TornInla$area.year <- seq(1,length(countyTorn))
formTypeI <- numberTorn~ + f(ID, model="bym", graph=tornb.inla)+
  f(Year, model="crw2") + f(Year2, model="iid")+
  f(area.year, model="iid")

mod.intI <- inla(formTypeI,family="poisson",data=TornInla,
                 control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE),
                 control.compute=list(dic=TRUE,cpo=TRUE))

--------------- type I works fine

#Type II
TornInla$area.int <http://area.int> <- TornInla$ID
TornInla$year.int <http://year.int> <- TornInla$Year

formTypeII <-numberTorn ~ + f(ID, model="bym", graph=tornb.inla)+
  f(Year, model= "rw2") + f(Year2, model="iid") +
  f(area.int <http://area.int>, model="iid", group = year.int <http://year.int>,
    control.group=list(model="rw2"))

mod.intII<-inla(formTypeII,family="poisson",data=TornInla,
                control.predictor=control$predictor,
                control.compute=list(dic=TRUE,cpo=TRUE))

----------------------throws an error:
Warning in inla(formTypeII, family = "poisson", data = TornInla, control.predictor = control$predictor,  :
  f(area.int <http://area.int>, ...) :  There is no indices where group[]=1, this is *usually* a misspesification
Warning in inla(formTypeII, family = "poisson", data = TornInla, control.predictor = control$predictor,  :
  f(area.int <http://area.int>, ...): Number of unused groups >= the number of groups used: 1969 >= 47, this is *usually* a misspesification
Error in inla.inlaprogram.has.crashed() :
  The inla-program exited with an error. Unless you interupted it yourself, please rerun with verbose=TRUE and check the output carefully.
  If this does not help, please contact the developers at <he...@r-inla.org>.
In addition: Warning message:
running command '"C:/Users/rp/Documents/R/win-library/3.3/INLA/bin/windows/64bit/inla.exe"  -b -s -v  "C:/Users/rp/AppData/Local/Temp/RtmpY3Jd2d/file1df8390cd9/Model.ini"' had status 1
>

#Type III
formTypeIII<- numberTorn~+ f(ID, model="bym", graph= tornb.inla)+
  f(Year, model="crw2") +
  f(Year2, model="iid") +
  f(year.int <http://year.int>, model="iid", group =area.int <http://area.int>,
    control.group=list(model="besag", graph = tornb.inla))

mod.intIII <- inla (formTypeIII,family="poisson",data=TornInla,
                    control.predictor=control$predictor,
                    control.compute=control$compute)

###Type IV
formTypeIV<- numberTorn ~+ f(ID, model="bym", graph=tornb.inla)+
  f(Year, model="crw2") + f(Year2, model="iid") +
  f(area.int <http://area.int>, control.group= list(model="rw2"))

mod.intIV <- inla (formTypeIV,family="poisson",data=TornInla,
                   control.predictor=control$predictor,
                   control.compute=control$compute)

Type III and IV just take too long (more than 12 hours so far). I even set in control.compute   openmp.strategy="huge", and I am running the scripts in MRO, which is supposelly faster than R, but still it isn't fast enough. Is this normal, or is there something wrong with the code? And why does it crash when I try to run the type II?
Any advice is welcome!

Thanks in advance,
Angela

messages.body_plain:
I'm comparing spatial predictions from a GAM to INLA/SPDE. The two images are from the same dataset, with splines on the left and INLA on the right. These come from a dataset of 3500 subjects predicted onto a dense regular grid with 60,000 coordinate pairs. The predictions and spatial heterogeneity are basically the same, but the INLA model is chunky and angular. I've tried a million different permutations, including different mesh density, different alpha values, and different prior values, and the INLA output is pretty much unchanged.

Would appreciate any advice getting a smoother output from INLA.

messages.body_plain:
Can you draw the mesh itself? You may even be able to overlay it with plot(mesh, add=TRUE)
That would show if it's the mesh triangles that are the direct cause or not. (It look like they are.)
Make sure you've experimented with substantially different meshes; max.edge only guarantees
the length of the longest edge, and the typical length is sometimes much smaller than that, so
that changing max.edge won't have any practical effect on the mesh resolution.  One option
is to set max.edge to a very small value and use the n.max parameter to control the computational
size of the mesh instead.  In either case, check what different mesh$n values your models have.

To get as smooth a field as the one on the left in your plot you need the triangles to be small enough
that the resulting piecewise linear field representation can be that smooth.  The closest I have to a
"safe" rule of thumb is that max.edge should be smaller than 10% of the effective correlation range.
(In many problems it can be larger, but that's model/problem dependent.)

Finn

> Predicting this onto a grid of 60,000 points takes a couple hours, but as best I can tell the model runs to completion. I've tried alpha values from 1.1 to 2.0 and there is no visible difference.

Unless your mesh has close to that many points, a faster alternative is to let inla do the prediction onto the mesh nodes mesh$loc only (use Diagonal(mesh$n) in the prediction stack), and use your A.pred matrix afterwards:

interpolatedpredictions <- data.frame(
  mean = A.pred %*% results$summary.linear.predictor[idx, "mean"]
  sd =A.pred %*% results$summary.linear.predictor[idx, "sd"]
)

The sd values obtain like that are essentially upper bounds on the sd in the interior of the triangles, and are nice to use when plotting the uncertainties.

Finn

On 23 January 2017 at 02:22, Paul Lantos <paul....@gmail.com> wrote:

> > bnd<-inla.nonconvex.hull(coords, convex=6000)
>
> > cmv.mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(
> +   boundary=bnd,
> +   max.edge=c(3000, 9000),
> +   cutoff=100)
>
> > cmv.spde<-inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh=cmv.mesh,
> +                               prior.range = c(0.3,0.4),
> +                               prior.sigma = c(100,0.5),
> +                               alpha=2.0)

This specifies a model where the mesh edges are only guaranteed to be 3km, but 40% of the prior probability mass for the range is only 0.3m, which is 10000 times too short to be resolved by the mesh!
 prior.range=c(3000, 0.01)
would likely give a different result...

Finn

messages.subject: Different levels of posterior standard deviation after re-scaling
messages.subject_clean: Different levels of posterior standard deviation after re-scaling
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I was trying to transform/re-scale the data to avoid big numbers in the fitting. However it was found that after re-scaling, the posterior mean seemed to be consistent across different scaling but the posterior standard deviation did not. For example, the data is z with sd. as roughly sigma. Then the fitted z/10 should be with sd. of roughly sigma/10 and after scaling back (z=(z/10)*10), the sd. should be sigma as well. But this didn't hold in the fitted SPDE model. May I ask why? How should we overcome this feature?

A simple example is attached below for illustration.
###############
# generate data and fit SPDE model
xy <- as.matrix(expand.grid(seq(0,1,0.05),seq(0,1,0.05)))
z <- 20*sin((xy[,1]+xy[,2])/20)
dmp <- matrix(c(0,0,0,1,1,1,1,0),4,2,byrow=T)
mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(,dmp,max.edge=c(0.05,0.1))
spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh,alpha=2)
A_est <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh,loc=xy)
stk_est1 <- inla.stack(data=list(resp=z),A=list(A_est),effects=list(i=1:spde$n.spde),tag='est1')
stk_est2 <- inla.stack(data=list(resp=z/20),A=list(A_est),effects=list(i=1:spde$n.spde),tag='est2')
stk_est3 <- inla.stack(data=list(resp=z*20),A=list(A_est),effects=list(i=1:spde$n.spde),tag='est3')
f_full <- resp ~ 0 + f(i,model=spde)
res1 <- inla(f_full,
            data=inla.stack.data(stk_est1),
            control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stk_est1)),
            control.compute=list(config = TRUE))
res2 <- inla(f_full,
            data=inla.stack.data(stk_est2),
            control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stk_est2)),
            control.compute=list(config = TRUE))
res3 <- inla(f_full,
            data=inla.stack.data(stk_est3),
            control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stk_est3)),
            control.compute=list(config = TRUE))
# generate posterior samples
nsamp <- 1000
zs1 <- inla.posterior.sample(nsamp,res1)
zs2 <- inla.posterior.sample(nsamp,res2)
zs3 <- inla.posterior.sample(nsamp,res3)
ind_i <- length(zs1[[1]]$latent)-spde$n.spde+(1:spde$n.spde)
zm1 <- zm2 <- zm3 <- matrix(NA,length(z),nsamp)
for(j in 1:nsamp){
  zm1[,j] <- drop(A_est%*%zs1[[j]]$latent[ind_i])
}
for(j in 1:nsamp){
  zm2[,j] <- drop(A_est%*%zs2[[j]]$latent[ind_i])
}
for(j in 1:nsamp){
  zm3[,j] <- drop(A_est%*%zs3[[j]]$latent[ind_i])
}

# true
summary(z)

# mean (similar)
summary(apply(zm1,1,mean))
summary(apply(zm2*20,1,mean))
summary(apply(zm3/20,1,mean))

# sd (different)
summary(apply(zm1,1,sd))
summary(apply(zm2*20,1,sd))
summary(apply(zm3/20,1,sd))

############# results ################
# true
> summary(z)
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.
 0.0000  0.6999  0.9996  0.9994  1.2990  1.9970
> # mean (similar)
> summary(apply(zm1,1,mean))
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.
0.00184 0.69990 0.99960 0.99940 1.29900 1.99500
> summary(apply(zm2*20,1,mean))
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.
 0.0176  0.6989  0.9997  0.9994  1.3000  1.9780
> summary(apply(zm3/20,1,mean))
     Min.   1st Qu.    Median      Mean   3rd Qu.      Max.
0.0000157 0.6998000 0.9996000 0.9994000 1.2990000 1.9970000
>
> # sd (different)
> summary(apply(zm1,1,sd))
    Min.  1st Qu.   Median     Mean  3rd Qu.     Max.
0.001443 0.001618 0.001704 0.001723 0.001822 0.002252
> summary(apply(zm2*20,1,sd))
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.
0.01265 0.01402 0.01442 0.01495 0.01522 0.02567
> summary(apply(zm3/20,1,sd))
     Min.   1st Qu.    Median      Mean   3rd Qu.      Max.
0.0001740 0.0002085 0.0002153 0.0002154 0.0002218 0.0002508

On 24 January 2017 at 11:12, Eridk Poliruyt <ep1...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi all,
>
> I was trying to transform/re-scale the data to avoid big numbers in the fitting. However it was found that after re-scaling, the posterior mean seemed to be consistent across different scaling but the posterior standard deviation did not. For example, the data is z with sd. as roughly sigma. Then the fitted z/10 should be with sd. of roughly sigma/10 and after scaling back (z=(z/10)*10), the sd. should be sigma as well. But this didn't hold in the fitted SPDE model. May I ask why? How should we overcome this feature?

The function you're testing with is essentially linear within the domain:
  library(fields)
  quilt.plot(xy[,1], xy[,2], z)
This leads to very large range estimates, with a large boundary effect, and the resulting adjustment needed for the variance parameter is possibly incompatible with the likelihood you have chosen (by using the "default" prior).  have you drawn any figures of the actual output? That is usually far more revealing than summary statistics, in particular if you're not sure your code is bug free.

Finn

On 24 January 2017 at 13:03, Eridk Poliruyt <ep1...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Thanks! The range was indeed too large. Would it help to extend the mesh (roughly twice the range?) ? Or it is not an ideal case for the SPDE model?

Well, model used (stationary field, no intercept) really isn't appropriate for the test data you had.
However, I notice that your test data was completely deterministic, which also doesn't play well with the observation likelihood, that includes random observation noise.  By changing the test case to

  z <- 20*sin((xy[,1]+xy[,2])/20) + rnorm(nrow(xy), 0.1)

the estimation becomes a lot more stable, and despite the estimated range baing a bit larger than the domain, the variance parameter estimates
actually does seem to scale in the way you intended, as well as the posterior predictions:

I'm happier with the output now -- I just needed to make the mesh finer. Too fine a mesh and I was getting a runtime error. This looks better with a ~ 22,000 point mesh.

I do have a couple questions that maybe you could help with --
 One, I've used the script you'd suggested to calculate a p value of sorts:

m.prd.1<- model1$summary.linear.predictor[inla.stack.index(stk.full, "prediction")$data,"mean"]
sd.prd.1<- model1$summary.linear.predictor[inla.stack.index(stk.full, "prediction")$data,"sd"]

pvalue1 <- 2*pmin(pnorm(m1, m.prd.1, sd.prd.1), 1-pnorm(m1, m.prd.1, sd.prd.1))

The significance I'm trying to calculate is where the pointwise odds differs from the average. I'd actually like a 2-tailed version where I can calculate areas where the odds are significantly lower than or significantly greater than the average. In my GAM scripts we do this with 1000 permutations, comparing the spatial to the non-spatial model model with an ANOVA. I recognize that statistical significance in a Bayesian context is a very different concept.

Another question has to do with random effects. I've got an "iid" term for geographic units from which I have multiple data points. To date the way I've typically looked for non-independence of geographic units has been a cluster analysis of model residuals. I suppose I could do that with semivariograms too. How would you recommend I do this using the INLA model output? How would I compare whether adding the "iid" term improves the model? I've seen some pretty nice visualizations of random effects plotted by slope and intercept (like on this linked page):

http://www.ats.ucla.edu/stat/r/dae/melogit.htm

Thanks for all the help,
Paul

Yes, that's the kind of probability calculated by that code; it doesn't distinguish between being lower/upper, but it detects both kinds of deviation.
If I recall correctly, it's the (posterior) probability
  P( |X-m| > |m.prd-m| )
when pretending that the overall mean m is known. This the connection to p-values as
"the probability of getting something this extreme or worse, if H0 is true", but from a
Bayesian perspective.

 If you want to be able to distinguish between lower/higher you need to do something slightly different ( like combining the "p-values" with sign(m-m.prd) )

messages.body_plain:
Units are in meters, as that is the unit of the CRS, but the prior.range and the max.edge match at least. I chose 1 km -- I think there is some heterogeneity at a fine spatial scale here. Would you suggest I go larger?

bnd<-inla.nonconvex.hull(coords, convex=5000)
cmv.mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(
  boundary=bnd,
  max.edge=c(1000, 4000),
  cutoff=250)
plot(cmv.mesh, asp=1, main="Mesh"); points(coords, col='red', pch=20, cex=0.5, main="Mesh")

cmv.spde<-inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh=cmv.mesh,
                              prior.range = c(1000,0.3),
                              prior.sigma = c(0.5,0.5),
                              alpha=2.0)

Fitted values are more or less similar between INLA (blue) and GAM (red), but the density distribution is different:

messages.body_plain:
You're still giving a large (30%) probability of a range shorter than the triangle edges.
Also, if you want to resolve features smaller than 1km you need smaller triangles.

The latest result plot also didn't look like it had been generated using the mesh you showed here; it shows linear features much larger than any triangle, so I still think you need to double check that you're plotting what you think you're plotting, by making simple plots in R before exporting to your other software.

Finn

Finn

messages.subject: Re: choice of priors for inla.spde.pcmatern
messages.subject_clean: choice of priors for inla.spde.pcmatern
messages.body_plain:
On Friday, 20 January 2017 17:40:22 UTC+1, Paul Lantos wrote:
> Hi again,
>  I'm trying to understand how the parameters are chosen for spde.pcmatern. It looks like the main parameters to specify are prior.range, prior.sd <http://prior.sd>, and alpha.
>
>  Is there a way to estimate appropriate values based on either my mesh or my primary data characteristics?
>
> A related question is that I'd like to understand how to evaluate whether the resulting model is over/under-smoothed, and how modifying these priors may help that.

Hi Paul,

The parameters "prior.range" and "prior.sd <http://prior.sd>" control the joint prior on range and standard deviation of the spatial field.

"prior.range" contains two values: range0 and Prange, such that the resulting prior satisfies P( range < range0) = Prange. The logic is that prior is constructed to "shrink" towards high values of range and that the user must select which ranges are so short that they are unfeasible for the problem at hand. For example, with range0 = 0.01 and Prange = 0.05 there is an a priori probability of only 5% that the range will be less than 0.01. From a theoretical point of view, it is challenging to come up with clear guidelines for how range0 and Prange should be selected, but, from a practical point of view, it is advisable not to favour ranges that are smaller than the resolution of the mesh. In the case that the range is similar to the edge lengths or smaller there are large discretisation errors in the SPDE model. However, the specification does not need to be based on the mesh size. If you have reason to believe that it is unreasonable that the range is less than, say 0.05, you would base the prior on that and not on a, potentially, much smaller triangle size in the mesh.

It is possible to force stronger smoothing (longer ranges) by making the prior on range stricter. For example, (range0 = 0.05, Prange = 0.05) will result in higher ranges than (range0 = 0.01, Prange = 0.05).

"prior.sigma" contains two values: sigma0 and Psigma, such that the resulting prior satisfies P(sigma > sigma_0) = Psigma. The logic is that the prior is constructed to shrink towards small values of the standard deviation for the spatial field and that the user must select which standard deviations for the spatial field that are so high that they are unfeasible for the problem at hand. This is dependent on the scaling of the data and the specific application so I do not know any clear guidelines to follow. If you have other similar data available, it could be used to come up with an idea about how large the spatial effect can be and then encode this into the prior by making standard deviation corresponding to unreasonably large spatial effects unlikely.

At this point I think one has to do some experimenting with the priors. As far as I know, we still do not have enough experience with the priors to come up with clearer guidelines.

Best regards,
Geir-Arne Fuglstad

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] control the number of knots
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] control the number of knots
messages.body_plain:
In the common GAMM packages like mgcv, the smooth models are defined as spline functions with a fixed, usually small, number of knots.
In INLA, the smooth models are handled more as Gaussian processes on continuous domains.
That means for example, that even though the meshes have a fixed number of "knots", this should not be used to control the smoothness of the model, but rather chosen so that the discrete model is able to represent whatever smoothness the continuous model leads to, and the parameters of the model (like the smoothing penalty for spline models; for spatial models usually also the correlation range parameter) is what controls the smoothness;
in spde models the triangles should be small enough that you don't see any obvious triangle patterns in the results.

In essence, it's like taking the limit k --> infinity, and making sure that the smoothing penalty is properly defined.
If your estimates of a rw2 model are less smooth than you think is reasonable, you can consider the prior settings for the model; you would then need to understand how to encode your "I think this is reasonable" information into that.

For 1D models, there _is_ however a way of achieving a similar "limited number of knots" effect using an SPDE version of the rw2 model, whih supports second order B-splines with limited number of knots.  The "Tokyo rainfall" example in the "read this first" SPDE tutorial on r-inla.org <http://r-inla.org> can be modified to produce such a model.  However, it's not something I would recommend, as models with a number of knots so small that it actually has an effect on the estimates is arguably needlessly artificial; the knot count and placement is a subjective model choice. In contrast, the continuous Gaussian process approach is non-parametric alternative.

Finn

The outcomes should be stored in a two-column matrix, with (at least) one NA entry for each row, so that the number of rows is the total number of observations; something like

observations <- rbind(cbind(Z, NA), cbind(NA, Y))

Ntrials should then be c(trials.z, trials.y)

You may also need
  control.predictor=list(link=c(rep(1, length(Z)), rep(2, length(Y))))
In your case both likelihoods have the same link function, but in general, this code is needed to tell
INLA which link function to apply for all-NA rows of "observations" for fitted.values output.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Dear

I read from Lindgren, Finn, and Håvard Rue (2008) paper the following statement
"The RW2 model is quite flexible due to its invariance to addition of a linear trend..." . From, the Bayesian Adaptive smoothing paper of Yu Ryan Yue et al, 2014, I read, "due to this property the result will coincide with result obtained by Wahba (1978) for the cubic smoothing spline".   I am not sure if I understand these two statements very well.

I did the following to check this (correct me if I am wrong)

# example data taken from Håvard Rue course on you tube
n=50
idx=1:n
fun=100*((idx-n/2)/n)^3
y=fun+rnorm(n,0,3)

formula7=y~f(idx,model="rw2",prior="loggamma",param=c(1,0.01))
r7 = inla(formula7,  data = list(y=y, idx=idx))

time<-idx   # I just create the copy of the location and assign to the new variable time

formula8=y~time+f(idx,model="rw2",prior="loggamma",param=c(1,0.01))
r8 = inla(formula8,  data = list(y=y, idx=idx))

plot(idx,y)
lines(r7$summary.random$idx$ID,r7$summary.random$idx$mean,col=2)
lines(r8$summary.random$idx$ID,r8$summary.random$idx$mean,col=4)

Following the addition of the linear line you will see a shift in the curve even though the behavior of the smooth curves are the same. Therefore, for some one who is using RW2 as an alternative to cubic spline, which approach is correct for use (r7 or r8).

Looking forward to hear from you
Kind regards
Belay

> Dear

> I read from Lindgren, Finn, and Håvard Rue (2008) paper the following statement
> "The RW2 model is quite flexible due to its invariance to addition of a linear trend..." . From, the Bayesian Adaptive smoothing paper of Yu Ryan Yue et al, 2014, I read, "due to this property the result will coincide with result obtained by Wahba (1978) for the cubic smoothing spline".   I am not sure if I understand these two statements very well.

Hi,
some answers below.

For question 1: The "density" p({x(t), all t}) for a rw2 process x(t) is unchanged if you add a linear trend: p({x(t)+a+bt, all t}) = p({x(t), all t})
This also means that it cannot be a true density; it's degenerate.

For question 2: In the continuous limit, the rw2 model on the interval (0,1) is characterised by

-2log p(x(.)) = C + \tau \int_{0,1} (d^2 x / dt^2)^2 dt

which is the same as the cubic spline penalty.  As a result, if a exact observations of x(t) are given at t1,t2,t3,...,tn, then the conditional expectation for x(t) under the rw2 model is exactly the same as the cubic spline interpolator.

> I did the following to check this (correct me if I am wrong)

Yes, I will correct you. ;-)
You were plotting only the rw2 component of the model. It's the combined effect of intercept, linear trend, and rw2 that should be the same (or close) for the two models, since the rw2 model can take up an arbitrary amount of the linear trend into itself due to the invariance property. A complicating factor is the possibility of including sum-to-zero constraints on the rw2 model and or slope=zero constraints, often imposed for the very reason that a linear trend and a free-ranging rw2 model are not mutually identifiable, due to the rw2 linear trend invariance.  The INLA implementation applies a sum-to-zero constrain to rw2 by default, but not a slope=0 constraint.  If the constraint is turned off, the automatic intercept term also needs to be turned off to avoid overparameterising the model.

Modified code showing the difference, and that all three models result in the same effective predictor:

n=50
idx=1:n
fun=100*((idx-n/2)/n)^3
y=fun+rnorm(n,0,3)

formula7=y~f(idx,model="rw2",prior="loggamma",param=c(1,0.01))

r7 = inla(formula7,  data = list(y=y, idx=idx),
          control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE))

time<-idx   # I just create the copy of the location and assign to the new variable time

formula8=y~time+f(idx,model="rw2",prior="loggamma",param=c(1,0.01))

r8 = inla(formula8,  data = list(y=y, idx=idx),
          control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE))

## Remove default constraint, and remove unneeded intercept
formula9=y~time+f(idx,model="rw2",prior="loggamma",param=c(1,0.01), constr=FALSE) -1
r9 = inla(formula9,  data = list(y=y, idx=idx),
          control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE))

par(mfrow=c(2,1))
plot(idx,y)
lines(r7$summary.random$idx$ID,r7$summary.random$idx$mean,col=2)
lines(r8$summary.random$idx$ID,r8$summary.random$idx$mean,col=4)
lines(r9$summary.random$idx$ID,r9$summary.random$idx$mean,col=5)

plot(idx,y)
lines(idx, r7$summary.linear.predictor$mean,col=2)
lines(idx, r8$summary.linear.predictor$mean,col=4)
lines(idx, r9$summary.linear.predictor$mean,col=5)

r7 = inla(formula7,  data = list(y=y, idx=idx),
          control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE))
r8 = inla(formula8,  data = list(y=y, idx=idx),
          control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE))

plot(idx,y)
lines(idx, r7$summary.linear.predictor$mean,col=2)
lines(idx, r8$summary.linear.predictor$mean,col=4)

messages.body_plain:
Thank you very much for that explanation. Choosing the prior.range seems clearer to me. I'm still uncertain as to how I'd guess the prior.sigma values. For instance how do I know what standard deviation would be unfeasible for the dataset?

Thanks,
Paul

On Wednesday, January 25, 2017 at 4:42:25 AM UTC-5, Geir-Arne Fuglstad wrote:
> On Friday, 20 January 2017 17:40:22 UTC+1, Paul Lantos wrote:
> > Hi again,
> >  I'm trying to understand how the parameters are chosen for spde.pcmatern. It looks like the main parameters to specify are prior.range, prior.sd <http://prior.sd>, and alpha.
> >
> >  Is there a way to estimate appropriate values based on either my mesh or my primary data characteristics?
> >
> > A related question is that I'd like to understand how to evaluate whether the resulting model is over/under-smoothed, and how modifying these priors may help that.
>
> Hi Paul,
>
> The parameters "prior.range" and "prior.sd <http://prior.sd>" control the joint prior on range and standard deviation of the spatial field.
>
> "prior.range" contains two values: range0 and Prange, such that the resulting prior satisfies P( range < range0) = Prange. The logic is that prior is constructed to "shrink" towards high values of range and that the user must select which ranges are so short that they are unfeasible for the problem at hand. For example, with range0 = 0.01 and Prange = 0.05 there is an a priori probability of only 5% that the range will be less than 0.01. From a theoretical point of view, it is challenging to come up with clear guidelines for how range0 and Prange should be selected, but, from a practical point of view, it is advisable not to favour ranges that are smaller than the resolution of the mesh. In the case that the range is similar to the edge lengths or smaller there are large discretisation errors in the SPDE model. However, the specification does not need to be based on the mesh size. If you have reason to believe that it is unreasonable that the range is less than, say 0.05, you would base the prior on that and not on a, potentially, much smaller triangle size in the mesh.
>
> It is possible to force stronger smoothing (longer ranges) by making the prior on range stricter. For example, (range0 = 0.05, Prange = 0.05) will result in higher ranges than (range0 = 0.01, Prange = 0.05).
>
> "prior.sigma" contains two values: sigma0 and Psigma, such that the resulting prior satisfies P(sigma > sigma_0) = Psigma. The logic is that the prior is constructed to shrink towards small values of the standard deviation for the spatial field and that the user must select which standard deviations for the spatial field that are so high that they are unfeasible for the problem at hand. This is dependent on the scaling of the data and the specific application so I do not know any clear guidelines to follow. If you have other similar data available, it could be used to come up with an idea about how large the spatial effect can be and then encode this into the prior by making standard deviation corresponding to unreasonably large spatial effects unlikely.
>
> At this point I think one has to do some experimenting with the priors. As far as I know, we still do not have enough experience with the priors to come up with clearer guidelines.
>
> Best regards,
> Geir-Arne Fuglstad

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Re: choice of priors for inla.spde.pcmatern
messages.body_plain:
That is a good question and I do not have a full answer for it. The problem is that if we are proper Bayesians, we should not look at the dataset when setting the priors. So we can't use the dataset itself to assess how much spatial variation there might be before we do the analysis.

However, we may have previous experience with similar phenomena. For example, if we are studying temperature measurements in Norway in, say June, I am quite sure most values will be in the range 0--25 degrees Celcius. The variation will be caused both by covariates and spatial variation and probably random effects such as a nugget, but the standard deviation of the spatial effect should probably be less than 6 and at least less than 10. So I would try something like sigma0 = 6 and Psigma = 0.05.

Obviously, this involved quite a bit of hand-waving. So I would experiment a bit with different values of sigma0 like 4 and 9 and see if things change substantially.

I think choosing sigma0 too high will have smaller consequences than choosing it too high. The prior on log(sigma) has a heavier left-hand side tail than right-hand side tail; choosing (sigma0 = 6, Psigma = 0.05) makes standard deviation equal to 6*2 = 12 far more unlikely than 6/2 = 3. So my intuition is that it is better to err on the side of a too loose upper limit rather than too strict.

--
Geir-Arne Fuglstad

messages.subject: Points off the spde grid
messages.subject_clean: Points off the spde grid
messages.body_plain:
Hi INLA,

I am trying to put together a space-time INLA model where I have a lot of data in harbours and along coastlines that I am trying to use to model the distribution of fish in the ocean. The problem is that when I create my mesh, the corner-cutting and approximation associated with the grid means that some of the points now lie outside the boundary of the domain - when I try to run the model, it simply stalls, and I think this is the reason why.

My questions are therefore
* How does INLA respond when there are observations outside of the domain?
* How can I filter my observations to limit them to only the ones within the domain?
* How can I best move the observations so the closest point within or on the boundary of the domain?

Cheers,

Mark

messages.subject: SPDE Default Prior
messages.subject_clean: SPDE Default Prior
messages.body_plain:
Dear Group,

I was asked to report the default SPDE prior generated by the inla.spde2.matern function. Can I report according to Lindgren & Rue (2015) as following?
1. the nominal range (rho) has a lognormal prior with mean natural logarithm of 20% of the mesh range, and precision 0.1;
2. the standard deviation (square root of the sill) has lognormal prior with mean log(1)=0 and precision 0.1 where 1 is the nominal prior standard deviation;
3. rho and sigma are a priori independent.

In  equation (2) Lindgren & Rue (2015), the exponent for 4\pi is d/2, but on page 12, R code line 5, the exponent for 4\pi is 1/2. Please explain the difference.
tau0 <- 1/(sqrt(4*pi) * kappa0 * sigma0)

I think inla.spde2.matern function uses 1/2 as the exponent.

Reference
Lindgren, Finn, and Håvard Rue. "Bayesian spatial modelling with R-INLA." Journal of Statistical Software 63.19 (2015).

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Points off the spde grid
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Points off the spde grid
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mark!

# Question 1
You cannot have observations outside the domain.

You can increase the mesh, so that you also have triangles on land. This is perfectly reasonable, as long as you don't do predictions or plotting on land. (The underlying spatial field exists there, but is never used).

# Q2
To filter your observations, the easiest is to create a spatial polygon from the mesh, and use "over".

# Q3
You can use the mesh$loc[ ,1:2] and find the nearest node, and put the observations at that node

I recommend increasing the mesh a bit to cover land.

Let me know if you need more help to do either of these.

Kind regards,
Haakon Bakka

messages.subject: Random terms in SPDE models
messages.subject_clean: Random terms in SPDE models
messages.body_plain:
These may be simple questions, but I'd appreciate some help -

 I'm interested in using neighborhood-level variables to predict individual level outcomes, which of course may violate an assumption of independence when multiple individuals come from the same neighborhood. To account for this I'm including an "iid" term in my models for each neighborhood identifier.

 Here are a few questions I've got as I develop these:

1 - There is certainly spatial autocorrelation of both individual values and neighborhood characteristics. If this is the case I'd suspect that the neighborhood-level random terms would not improve my modeling much when I already account for individual correlation (in the SPDE construct right?).

 I don't know of a better way to compare, but here are the DIC values for different versions of the model. My interpretation is that once individual spatial relationships enter the model via the SPDE, the random effects for neighborhood identifier become trivial. So the question becomes 1) is DIC sufficient to compare these models? and 2) If I'm using some neighborhood level fixed effect (like neighborhood poverty level to predict individual outcome) should I retain the random term?

No SPDE, no random terms:
y ~ 0 + b0
Deviance Information Criterion (DIC) ...: 4812.35

No SPDE, random term added for neighborhood ("fips" identifier):
y ~ 0 + b0 + f(fips, model="iid")
Deviance Information Criterion (DIC) ...: 4798.34

SPDE included, no random effects:
y ~ 0 + b0 + f(s, model=spde)
Deviance Information Criterion (DIC) ...: 4713.17

SPDE plus random effects:
y ~ 0 + b0 + f(s, model=cmv.spde) + f(fips, model="iid")
Deviance Information Criterion (DIC) ...: 4713.14

2. Typically I would compare these models by looking at spatial autocorrelation of residuals, so collect the residual values for each level of the fixed term and do something like a local Moran's. If the residuals are for each individual, then I could compute an average within each neighborhood unit. Is that the right approach for this model as well? I'm not quite sure how to access the residuals from the INLA output and attach them to the original data points, however.

3. Similarly I've seen some visualizations of random effects where the slopes and intercepts can be stacked graphically or mapped. See this as an example of graphing them (in this case from a GLMM): http://www.ats.ucla.edu/stat/r/dae/melogit.htm

Is there a straightforward way to collect the random slopes and intercepts by neighborhood identifier?

Thanks!

Dear INLA developers,

Good morning.

I tried the sample scripts of the spatial lag model and implemented these scripts to my dataset as well. The problem is the predicted values are too good to be trusted because R^2 values are always very close to 1. Please look at the sample scripts of the spatial lag model below:

> require(INLA)
> require(spdep)
> data(boston)
> n <- nrow(boston.c)
> boston.c$idx <- 1:n
> lw <- nb2listw(boston.soi)
> W <- as(as_dgRMatrix_listw(lw), "CsparseMatrix")
> f1 <- log(CMEDV) ~ CRIM + ZN + INDUS
> mmatrix <- model.matrix(f1, boston.c)
> zero.variance = list(prec=list(initial = 25, fixed=TRUE))
> e = eigenw(lw)
> re.idx = which(abs(Im(e)) < 1e-6)
> rho.max = 1/max(Re(e[re.idx]))
> rho.min = 1/min(Re(e[re.idx]))
> rho = mean(c(rho.min, rho.max))
> betaprec <- .0001
> Q.beta = Diagonal(n=ncol(mmatrix), betaprec)
> hyper = list(
+   prec = list(
+     prior = "loggamma",
+     param = c(0.01, 0.01)),
+   rho = list(
+     initial=0,
+     prior = "logitbeta",
+     param = c(1,1)))## Fit model
> slmm1 <- inla( log(CMEDV) ~ -1 +
+                  f(idx, model="slm",
+                    args.slm=list(
+                      rho.min = rho.min,
+                      rho.max = rho.max,
+                      W=W,
+                      X=mmatrix,
+                      Q.beta=Q.beta),
+                    hyper=hyper),
+                data=boston.c, family="gaussian",
+                control.predictor=list(compute=T),
+                control.family = list(hyper=zero.variance),
+                control.compute=list(dic=TRUE, cpo=TRUE)
+ )
> fit.slm <- slmm1$summary.fitted.values[1]
> cor(fit.slm, log(boston.c$CMEDV))^2
     [,1]
mean    1

If we look at R^2 of the regular spatial lag model and the linear regression model, we can see R^2 values are only 0.77 and 0.41.
## spatial lag model
> m2 <- lagsarlm(f1, boston.c, lw)
> cor(predict(m2), log(boston.c$CMEDV))^2
[1] 0.7734959

## linear regression
> summary(lm1 <- lm(f1, data=boston.c))

F-statistic: 120.4 on 3 and 502 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

I tried the spatial error model, spatial lag model, and spatial Durbin model from INLABMA package as well, all of them have R^2 close to 1 no matter which dataset and which likehoods I used. My dataset has R^2 around 0.16 when I used GLM function with binomial regression model. However, the R^2 value increases dramatically to 0.9998 if I use INLA spatial lag model. messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: Random terms in SPDE models
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Re: Random terms in SPDE models
messages.body_plain:
Can you specify your likelihood also?

Some general answers:
- You can include both iid and spatial effects, as long as you use pc priors with some shrinkage. Look at the posterior standard deviations and see whether you need the components
- DIC is known to be bad for models with many parameters. Does anyone have a solid citation for this?
- You can try to use the cpo instead of DIC or WAIC

2. The iid residuals are usually in inla.result$summary.random$...
- Except if you mean the likelihood residuals

PS: I think some of your questions are a bit "out of scope" of what you can expect to be answered by the INLA team. Of course, anyone is welcome to discuss these questions!

Kind regards,
Haakon

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

the issue is that the slm model moves the whole model, including the
likelihood, into the latent field, and hence the 'predicted' and
'fitted' values one normally use, does not make sense. You'll also see
from the code that the gaussian response has essetially zero variance.
you have to use the values from within the slm model itself. VIRGILIO
GOMEZ RUBIO <Virgili...@uclm.es>  knows details here...

Best,
H

On Sun, 2017-01-29 at 07:52 -0800, Anna wrote:
> Dear INLA developers,
>
> Good morning.
>
> I tried the sample scripts of the spatial lag model and implemented
> these scripts to my dataset as well. The problem is the predicted
> values are too good to be trusted because R^2 values are always very
> close to 1. Please look at the sample scripts of the spatial lag
> model below:
>
> > require(INLA)
> > require(spdep)
> > data(boston)
> > n <- nrow(boston.c)
> > boston.c$idx <- 1:n
> > lw <- nb2listw(boston.soi)
> > W <- as(as_dgRMatrix_listw(lw), "CsparseMatrix")
> > f1 <- log(CMEDV) ~ CRIM + ZN + INDUS
> > mmatrix <- model.matrix(f1, boston.c)
> > zero.variance = list(prec=list(initial = 25, fixed=TRUE))
> > e = eigenw(lw)
> > re.idx = which(abs(Im(e)) < 1e-6)
> > rho.max = 1/max(Re(e[re.idx]))
> > rho.min = 1/min(Re(e[re.idx]))
> > rho = mean(c(rho.min, rho.max))
> > betaprec <- .0001
> > Q.beta = Diagonal(n=ncol(mmatrix), betaprec)
> > hyper = list(
> +   prec = list(
> +     prior = "loggamma",
> +     param = c(0.01, 0.01)),
> +   rho = list(
> +     initial=0,
> +     prior = "logitbeta",
> +     param = c(1,1)))## Fit model
> > slmm1 <- inla( log(CMEDV) ~ -1 +
> +                  f(idx, model="slm",
> +                    args.slm=list(
> +                      rho.min = rho.min,
> +                      rho.max = rho.max,
> +                      W=W,
> +                      X=mmatrix,
> +                      Q.beta=Q.beta),
> +                    hyper=hyper),
> +                data=boston.c, family="gaussian",
> +                control.predictor=list(compute=T),
> +                control.family = list(hyper=zero.variance),
> +                control.compute=list(dic=TRUE, cpo=TRUE)

> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > 2. I'm not quite sure how to access the residuals from the INLA output and attach them to the original data points, however.
> > > > >

> > > > > 3. Similarly I've seen some visualizations of random effects where the slopes and intercepts can be stacked graphically or mapped. See this as an example of graphing them (in this case from a GLMM): http://www.ats.ucla.edu/stat/r/dae/melogit.htm

messages.subject: CHEKING VERBOSE
messages.subject_clean: CHEKING VERBOSE
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA users,

I am trying to fit a model with eight hyperparameters, one for the precision of the gaussian response, 5 for the different precision effects of the random walks, and two for the spatial effect. INLA seems to work right, but I have two questions about the results:

1. The first one is related with the VERBOSE. When I check the convergence of the method, I check three things:
     1.1. INLA doesn't give the message "Mode not sufficient accurate; switch to a stupid local search strategy."
     1.2. The eigenvalues of the Hessian matrix are not so big.
     1.3. The values of the Compute corrected stdev for the hyperparameters are between 0.5 and 1.5.
Please, correct me if I have mistakes :) . Now, I am continuously getting  "Mode not sufficient accurate; switch to a stupid local search strategy",  but the rest of conditions seems correct and the results seem to make sense. I have modified the priors, and the results are always the same and the message appears again. My question is, Can I trust in this result despite of the message? I enclose the verbose.

2. The second one is related with the number of hyperparameters, In the paper Rue et al. (2009), the number of hyperparameters recommended is less than 6. However, here we have 8 hyperparameters, and INLA works despite of the previous message. Should I reduce the number of hyperparameters?

Thanks for everything!!! :)

Joaquín.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Anna,

In addition to what Havard has said, we are aware of this issue. Roger Bivand reported that  some time ago and I am trying to find out what is going on. Please, note that the slm latent effect is still marked as experimental for a reason...

In principle, for Gaussian models the estimates of the different parameters are very accurate, so I think that an alternative way to obtain the fitted values is to compute a linear combination on the parameters using the actual values of the covariates. Perhaps Havard can correct me here.

For non-Gaussian models we still need to conduct more tests as I am not sure we are using the same link function as other implementations...

I am developing an R package that includes some JAGS code to fit some Spatial Econometrics models to carry out all these comparissons. It is slow but I am using it to compare INLA and MCMC. You can find it here:

https://github.com/becarioprecario/SEjags

There is a doc (still under development) comparing results with INLA and MCMC under SEjags/inst/doc.

You can install the whole package using:

install_github("becarioprecario/SEjags")

Hope this helps.

Virgilio

messages.body_plain:
Hi Anna,

please, check the vignette in the SEjags package. You can install the package and browse it doing this:

devtools::install_github("becarioprecario/SEjags")
library(SEjags)
browseVignettes("SEjags")

Note that, at the moment, the documentation is incomplete and it may change, but it will show you how to compute the fitted values using linear combinations. Also, it seems as if the marginals computed with INLA and MCMC are the same but that the summary statistics are not.

Best,

Virgilio
